one_liner: Safe pure-Rust succinct structures (Rank9Sel, DArray, Elias-Fano, wavelet matrix); select1 1.3-7.8x faster than vers-vecs on ARM64.
what_it_does: A curated crate of succinct data structures in four groups: bit vectors with rank/select (BitVector, Rank9Sel, DArray, SArray), compressed integer vectors (CompactVector, DACs), monotone sequences (Elias-Fano) and character sequences (wavelet matrix). Structures in a group share the Access/Rank/Select/Build traits so they can be swapped, and every structure serializes through a Serializable trait. Queries return Option (None when out of range) rather than panicking.
how_it_is_fast: Rank9Sel is Vigna's rank9: per 512-bit block one 64-bit absolute rank plus seven 9-bit sub-block ranks packed into one word, so rank1 is two loads and a popcount. select1 uses optional hints (one per 1024 ones) to narrow a binary search over block ranks, then a broadword parallel compare over the packed 9-bit counts picks the word, and an in-word select finishes with broadword byte sums plus a 2 KB select-in-byte lookup table (no PDEP). The `intrinsics` feature swaps the broadword popcount and bit scans for count_ones/trailing_zeros, which compile to hardware instructions (the docs recommend -C target-cpu=native with it).
when_to_use: Static bit vectors of millions of bits where you need rank1 and select1 from one structure and want a code base with no unsafe memory tricks.
select-heavy workloads on ARM64: in the succinctly comparison sucds' select1 beat vers-vecs and succinctly at every size and density tested (1M and 10M bits, 10-90% density).
Projects that need several succinct families (Elias-Fano, DACs, wavelet matrix) behind one consistent trait API and a built-in serialization format.
no_std targets with alloc (supported since 0.9.0), and portable builds where the serialized format must not depend on pointer width.
when_not_to_use: Peak rank/select speed: sux-rs was faster on both rank1 (about 1.5-1.85x) and select1 in the same tables.
Memory-tight bit vectors: rank9 alone costs 25% over the raw bits by design; vers-vecs measured 5-6.5% total overhead against sucds' 36% at 1M bits.

When you already hold the data as Vec<u64> and build often: there is no constructor that adopts a word vector, so you copy it in (word-at-a-time push_bits works; bit-at-a-time from_bits is far slower).

Loading untrusted serialized files: deserialize_from does not check that the stored length matches the word count or that the index belongs to the vector, and Vec deserialization reserves the stored length up front, so a crafted file can trigger a huge allocation or later index panics.
If you need RRR, balanced parentheses or an FM-index: these are open feature requests (#13, #17, #27), not implemented.

integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.62 (rust-version in Cargo.toml for 0.9.x; 1.61 for 0.8.x), edition 2018
integration.platforms: any; tuned for 64-bit, 32-bit support (broadword emulation, under 2^32 bits) merged on 2026-08-31 after the 0.9.1 release
integration.thread_safety: not documented; query methods take &self on plain Vec-backed structs, so immutable sharing across threads follows normal Rust Send/Sync rules
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: shares the conceptual rank/select API of other Rust crates but uses its own Rank/Select traits returning Option<usize>; not a drop-in for vers-vecs, sux or SDSL

gotchas: Rank9Sel::from_bits does not build select hints; call .select1_hints() (and .select0_hints()) or select falls back to a full binary search over all blocks.

BitVector::from_bits pushes bit by bit into a growing Vec and never calls shrink_to_fit, so resident memory can be up to about 2x the bits: this matches the benchmark's 99% overhead at 10M bits (156,250 words rounded up to a 262,144-word capacity plus the 25% rank directory), against 36% at 1M bits. Build with BitVector::with_capacity and push_bits(word, 64), or shrink before indexing.

Rank9SelIndex::rank1/select1 are `unsafe fn` only as an API contract (you must pass the same BitVector used at construction); the crate itself uses bounds-checked safe Rust, and a mismatched vector gives wrong answers or a panic rather than memory corruption.
Even with `intrinsics`, in-word select does not use BMI2 PDEP/TZCNT on x86-64, so select1 leaves some x86 speed on the table compared with PDEP-based implementations.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick sucds over sux-rs when you want a small, dependency-free, no_std-capable crate with a broad family of structures and no unsafe internals, and can accept slower rank1/select1; pick vers-vecs when space (5-6.5% overhead) or fast construction from Vec<u64> matters more than select speed; QWT (Rust) is the better choice for wavelet trees over larger alphabets.
verified_claims_summary: succinctly's own cross-crate benchmark (rustc 1.97.0, criterion, default bench profile, Apple M5 Max ARM64) timed 10,000 random select1 queries on identical seeded 1M- and 10M-bit vectors: sucds 0.8.3 Rank9Sel with `intrinsics` took 70.8-139.7 us against 174.4-575.6 us for vers-vecs RsVec (scalar select on ARM64) and 181.0-279.8 us for succinctly BitVec, while rank1 was level with succinctly and about 2x faster than vers-vecs; sux-rs beat it on both.
status_note: Actively maintained by Shunsuke Kanda (0.9.1 on 2026-08-29, breaking 0.9.0 API changes on 2026-08-28, 32-bit support merged 2026-08-31, about 950k crates.io downloads), dual MIT/Apache-2.0 safe pure Rust, so it is easy to depend on or vendor.
